It's discrimination, but it's reasonable discrimination. Pulling straight from the article:

  • 71% of all car accident-related deaths in 2012 were males.

  • The number of drivers who died in a fatal car accident was 50% higher for men than women in 2008.

  • Men are much more likely to have been under the influence of alcohol in a fatal crash. In 2012, 38% of fatally injured male drivers had BACs of over 0.08%, as compared to 20% of fatally injured female drivers.

  • Seat belt use was observed in 88% of female front seat occupants, as compared to 84% of male front seat occupants.

  • In 2012, 23% of male drivers who were involved in fatal accidents were speeding at the time of the accident, while 14% of women involved in fatal crashes were doing the same.

This has nothing to do with caring. It's just a fact that insuring male drivers is a larger financial risk than insuring female drivers.

Discrimination as a matter of law is terrible, but there is a reason for a private insurance company to discriminate in this way. It is perfectly rational.

Let's say John is a man, and any given man has a 15% chance of getting in an accident this year. As his insurer, I have to pay John a large sum of money if he gets in an accident. In return, John pays me a much smaller premium every month to make sure he's covered. If John is my only customer, even though statistically the premium should leave me profiting, I'm taking a huge gamble on him not crashing. But with tens of thousands of clients, the risk gets spread out and I charge John and other men a rate based on the data from his demographic.

But then comes Sarah. Let's pretend a given woman has only a 5% chance of getting in an accident this year. It's less risky for me to insure Sarah than John, because there is a lower chance of me as the insurer having to pay out a large claim. If Sarah costs less to insure (by way of risk analysis) it would make no sense to charge her John's premium for the sake of equality.

In fact, John's premium is calculated based on what he's willing to pay with respect to his risk. Sarah, being less likely to get in an accident, literally does not value insurance as highly as John. If she was charged John's rate it might make more sense for her to just put a sum of money in an account every month and deal with things herself.

I don't want Sarah to do this because I stand to profit by insuring her, even if I charge her a lower premium. So instead, I charge her a price that corresponds to her lower valuation of insurance.

Price discrimination is the cornerstone of insurance. Why should a healthy person have to pay the same for life insurance as an obese chain smoker? At those prices it wouldn't make economic sense for the healthy guy.

Is a wage gap unfair or wrong if more men are willing to risk life and limb on an oil rig, in construction, in combat than women?

The law should regard everyone equally, but that doesn't mean every agent in an economy should.
